title: PlayStation defeats $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over game pricing
author: Christopher Dring
excerpt: London Tribunal rules that Sony doesn’t have a ‘near monopoly’ on game sales

PlayStation defeats $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over game pricing
London Tribunal rules that Sony doesn’t have a ‘near monopoly’ on game sales
Christopher Dring
Nov 17
Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.
The lawsuit was brought about by Alex Neill, who is representing consumers that purchased PlayStation digital content between August 2016 and February 2026. The action accused PlayStation of having a ‘near monopoly’ on digital games and add-on content on PlayStation platforms. The case argued that Sony sets strict terms and conditions on developers, and charges a 30% commission on every purchase, which results in “excessive and unfair prices”. It claimed the prices are out of proportion to the costs.
But London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected this, and said the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law. As a result, it has dismissed the case in its entirety.
The lawsuit argued that once you own a PlayStation, you are trapped within the ecosystem. The Tribunal disagreed, and ruled that Sony competes within a wider ‘systems market’ with the likes of Xbox, Nintendo and PC. It also ruled that gamers can buy physical games (at least for now).
The court said that forcing PlayStation to allow third-party stores onto the platform would be expensive, complex and could impact security. It added that under competition law, there was no legal duty for Sony to do this.
Finally, the court didn’t find pricing to be unfair. It said that Alex Neill had failed to prove Sony’s profit margins were excessive, especially as console makers sell hardware cheaply to make money back on game sales. Furthermore, there tribunal said there no evidence that rival stores would have brought pricing down.
PlayStation still faces similar class actions in Australia, Netherlands and Portugal at an earlier stage.
For more details on the Alex Neill case, you can read our run-down from earlier this year.

The boss who launched GTA 4 and Red Dead Redemption: “AAA is under threat”
Leading games VC Ben Feder explains why $300m budgets aren’t sustainable, and why AI just needs its “Toy Story moment”
Christopher Dring
Nov 17
In This Edition,
Tirta Ventures’ Ben Feder on…
Why now is the time to back start-ups
The problem with AAA
AI’s ‘Toy Story moment’
Napster-level disruption in games
Even though it’s been over 15 years since he ran Take-Two, Ben Feder is feeling nostalgic on the eve of the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6.
“ It’s a great time to be at Take-Two,” he tells us. “It’s really great when you don’t know the outcome and it’s a huge success. In this particular case, I feel like we know the outcome. Everybody on the team, I’m sure, has been waiting a long time for this moment. It’s going to be an amazing launch. I am a little wistful. But I’m happy for everybody there.”
Feder was at Take-Two for the launch of GTA 4, Red Dead Redemption, BioShock and Borderlands. He also successfully steered the company away from EA’s bid to acquire it, because he believed Take-Two’s IP and talent held “substantial unrealized value”. It was a belief that has been proven right many times over, and will be again when GTA 6 arrives this week.
Feder, now the head of games VC fund Tirta Ventures, knows that GTA 6 is the exception to the rule. For the rest of the industry, the reality is constant waves of layoffs, studio closures and anxiety around the future direction of the business. Nevertheless, he’s optimistic.
“There is obviously consolidation at the mature side of the industry,” he acknowledges. “There are a lot of layoffs. There’s competition from other sources of attention-grabbing content like TikTok, YouTube, micro-dramas, and the like. And technology is having a thing right now. For guys like me investing in innovation, that’s an incredible opportunity.
“I would not say it’s a crisis, I would say it’s a significant transition. Gaming spent decades disrupting other forms of entertainment, and now we’re competing with everyone for 30 minutes of somebody’s life.
“If you’re working in the industry as an engineer, an artist, an animator, you’re a little nervous, You’ve seen round and round of layoffs. But I’d like to think there’s a healthy part to all of this, which is cost rationalization on the one hand and huge revenue upside on the other. But it’s definitely an industry in transition, without question.”
The $300m time capsule
By the time Concord came out, the world had changed
This brutal transition is causing problems across the ecosystem, from indie projects to large-scale live-service games. But Feder feels it’s the AAA space that faces the biggest challenge.
“Around content, AAA is under the most amount of threat. They’re not big enough to really be platforms on the one hand, and they’re not small enough to really innovate on the other. If you talk to the major publishers, they cannot figure out a way to make a game for less than $300 million, and that to me is just not sustainable.”
He continues: “Greenlighting a $300 million game that takes five years is as if you’re taking your entire development team, putting them in a time capsule, burying them in the ground, and five years later they pop out and say, ‘Voila, here it is.’
“Three to five years ago, that was reasonable because we know what they’re building, it’s good IP, they have a niche, and we know what the world’s going to look like when they pop out of the ground. Today, while they’re underground, on the surface of planet Earth all of this change is happening, not just technologically but also with respect to consumer tastes and expectations. They may come out five years from now, and the world may not care.”
GTA 6 is an example of a AAA title that managed to migrate from game to platform and deliver “escape velocity”. It’s a very difficult feat to pull off.
“Scale matters there, and you need an enormous amount of capital to do that,” Feder notes. “The amount of capital required starts with a ‘B’ not with an ‘M’, for sure.”
This reality means that the established AAA publishers are increasingly leaning on bankable, existing IP and communities.
“They may come out five years from now, and the world may not care.”
So far, this is quite a negative analysis. But it’s here where Feder is optimistic. If the established game companies are unable to disrupt the market, that provides an opportunity for new businesses, particularly in this age of AI. And that’s where Feder and his team are investing.
“If you look historically, every major shift in technology creates a tailwind for start-ups and entrepreneurs to create multi-billion-dollar companies. We believe the next generation of those companies are being formed right now.
“I was at Epic for a little while, and one of the things that enabled Fortnite was technology that wasn’t available earlier. Putting 100 people in a single instance of a game to play against each other wasn’t possible ten years earlier. That was a result, in part, of technological innovation.
“We believe this current technological wave, the mother of all waves, is going to lead to new types of enterprises and new types of companies.”
Feder suggests that established companies are not particularly well-placed to capitalize on this shift.
“A lot of incumbents think about AI as a way of reducing costs, which it is. I query whether it will actually reduce costs, or will it just make games bigger for the same cost? But we’re more interested in what AI can do to radically change gameplay.
“That’s question number one as we think about what we invest in: Was this possible before AI? And when AI gets better, does the game get better? That’s harder for an incumbent to focus on, because they deploy a lot of capital, have enormous advantages in terms of distribution, capital, and IP, and all of that needs to be protected.”
Feder believes that the established giants are happy for these start-ups to do the disrupting, as they can always buy them afterwards.
“They’re happy that venture firms like ours are funding entrepreneurs to create new types of IP. Because once we’ve proven that IP can be valuable, in theory, they’re willing to pay up for it later. They’re just using the whole venture environment as your R&D lab. It’s not a terrible way to approach it.”
AI’s Toy Story Will Bring Acceptance
Feder argues that the best time to debut new IP is during times of technological change. It used to be that a good time to try a new concept was at the launch of new consoles, for instance.
“Because there’s new capabilities, there’s also new types of content available, and consumers got excited about it,” he explains. “When they open their minds, they open their hearts. And when they open their hearts, they open their wallets. That to me is the time to develop new IP.”
He suggests we view ChatGPT as the “accidental consumer technology group” that will lead to new types of experiences from new companies. And as a result, Tirta has invested a lot in AI-first game businesses.
But do consumers really want this? Gamers, certainly in the West, are openly hostile to AI in their games.
Feder acknowledges this is a challenge, but believes we’re one special launch away from that changing
“When animation went from hand-drawn to computer animation, there was a massive wall of resistance,” he says. “People didn’t think it looked good. Then Pixar launched Toy Story. They created a movie that not only was awesome, but used computer-generated animation and chose a subject matter that made the most of it, and did an amazing job with it. Once Toy Story launched, all the resistance went away. My own view is that we are one Toy Story moment away from consumer acceptance of AI in video games in the West. In the East, they’ve already accepted it.”
Our Napster moment?
One area of AI that has caught Feder’s attention is the rise of decompilations, which we covered this earlier in the month. It’s the act of people using AI to decompile games and rebuild them in new ways.
It’s potentially a threat to game companies that do not want their titles broken down, rebuilt and distributed in unintended ways. And Feder believes this could have significant repercussions, comparing it to the impact of Napster on the music business.
“ The music business used to rely on its IP. Every time there was a technological shift, there was a giant opportunity to basically resell your entire catalogue. If you went from cassette to CD, people tended to rebuy all of their music. Then Napster came along and everybody’s catalogue was basically stolen.
“Never mind the lawsuits, eventually the music industry migrated first to live entertainment as a way to get around that issue, and then ultimately to streaming. The illegality of it is super problematic, but if you put that to the side for a second, gamers are intrigued by this idea of being able to mix content, remix it, and try different things. They really create with it.
“You need to pay attention to what that really means and what consumers want, and see if you can figure out a way to do it in a legal way. It creates a huge challenge for the industry. I’m sure the incumbents will respond because I don’t think they’re going to let their IP just be stolen like that. That said, I do expect to see a lot of mixing, and in that world, live ops are going to be important.”
Surviving the transition
We end our chat with Feder by asking him two questions. First, as a former leader of Take-Two and Tencent, what would Feder do if he were leading a big company in this current turbulent market?
“You need to protect your core, and then grow from there,” he answers. “The core ultimately goes down to your IP, your creative talent, your communities, and your distribution. That’s critically important.
“If I were restructuring a major publisher, I wouldn’t do what I’m doing, chasing everything. I would advise people to start skunkworks and see what you can do with these new tools. Start from first principles and develop it from scratch.
“When you’re a big publisher and you have a five-year development cycle, and you’re trying to introduce new technologies and new processes in the middle of all that, it’s impossible. What you need to do is establish smaller, autonomous teams to experiment with new technologies, see what they can do, take some risks, and maybe you get lucky and hit upon something new.”
And then finally, what advice would he give to those new start-ups and founders at the other end of the spectrum?
“You should ignore all conventional wisdom,” he concludes. “First and foremost, don’t lose sight of the audience and don’t lose sight of the game. All of the technology stuff is interesting, but at the end of the day, you need to delight consumers.
“Start with a compelling creative vision and a clear understanding of why players will care about whatever you’re building. I would not assume an ambitious game requires large teams, or enormous budgets, or lengthy development cycles. That can all be rethought. And use AI to rethink development, not simply to automate existing workflows, because workflows are also going to change. I’d build early, I’d test frequently, I’d learn from the players, and I’d think about distribution and community from the ground up.
“As content becomes easier to produce, taste matters, originality matters, authentic engagement becomes more valuable than ever, and authority matters. All the things that go into making really great IP and really great experiences become much more front and center, as opposed to workflows and technology, which fade to the backend.”
Check out our full chat with Ben Feder in today’s edition of The Game Business Show.
